A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EchoVLA and MoMani, with readable and matchable text, equations, tables, and figures. V1 includes Appendices A–F; v2 ends after its references. Appendix omissions can be distinguished from material incorporated into v2's main text.

before.justification: V1 reports original RoboCasa evaluations, modality and memory ablations, real-robot experiments, and additional microwave-knob results in Appendix F.

after.justification: V2 reports original simulation results, ablations, memory-parameter sensitivity experiments, and six-task real-robot evaluations in Tables 2–5.

M1.justification: EchoVLA's encoders, memory updates, retrieval, per-part diffusion policies, and loss remain unchanged. However, v2 replaces MoMani's brief generate-execute-repair description with a two-stage pipeline including quality gates, offline top-K selection, and auditing. The PDFs do not resolve whether these are procedural changes or previously undocumented details.

E1.justification: V2 adds EnP, involving cross-room navigation and placing pears on a cabinet. The existing simulation tasks and real-world tasks remain represented. Microwave-knob rotation already appeared in v1 Appendix F, and TC becomes PCIS without changing the cup-to-sink task.

E2.justification: V2 omits DP3 from the real-world comparisons reported in v1 Appendix F, including the RK table and results described for other tasks. The RoboCasa comparator set is unchanged. BSC-Nav and the platforms in v2 Table 1 are positioning comparisons, not newly evaluated policy baselines.

E3.justification: V2 Table 4 introduces experiments varying episodic-memory window size over 2, 4, 8, and 16 and update threshold over 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7 on PnPC2S Mobile. The retained RoboCasa task setup, success-rate metric, and 50-episode evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original modality and memory ablations are retained, and v2 adds two memory-parameter sensitivity analyses. Conversely, it removes v1's trajectory-length comparisons and voxel-map construction, alignment, and retrieval diagnostics from Appendices C–E. This substantially changes the supporting analyses; the new noise and occlusion discussion does not constitute a separate controlled robustness experiment.

E5.justification: V2 first specifies 20 independent real-world trials per task with randomized initial base positions. This is newly reported repetition information, not evidence of increased runs. Simulation reporting remains three seeds and 50 episodes; neither version supplies confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Between v1 Table 1 and v2 Table 2, π0.5's manipulation/navigation average changes from 0.44 to 0.32, while EchoVLA's simulation averages remain 0.52 and 0.31. V2 adds sensitivity results and EnP success rates of 0.10, 0.00, and 0.03 for EchoVLA, π0.5, and Diffusion Policy. Existing real-task scores, including RK, are retained; EchoVLA's real-world average changes from 0.51 to 0.44 because the aggregate expands from four to six tasks. Appendix trajectory statistics and real-world DP3 results are removed.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9 retain the same policy formulation, multimodal tokens, voxel representation, episodic buffer, attention operations, and diffusion objective. Neither version adds theoretical propositions or proofs; the new experimental thresholds do not introduce mathematical results.

C1.justification: The central dual-memory VLA and automated benchmark contributions remain. The abstract strengthens the quantified manipulation/navigation advantage over π0.5 from 0.08 to 0.20, without changing EchoVLA's score. Section 4 also adds an explicit exclusivity claim about MoMani combining automated generation modes with simulated and real-robot data.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations involving plan forgetting, stale scene memory, episodic compensation for spatial errors, and refrigerator-door occlusion. Limitations expand from noisy depth to pose errors, odometry drift, and voxel-map ghosting. Meanwhile, v1's task-complexity interpretation, DP3 normalization explanation, and observation of attention to the robot's own body are omitted. These materially revise the mechanism and failure discussion.

D1.justification: V2 removes v1's complete training recipe, including AdamW, learning rate, batch size, epochs, warm-up, regularization, and diffusion-step count, along with detailed object dimensions and camera placement. It adds memory settings L=8 and τ=0.5 and data-generation details such as alignment tolerances of 0.05 m and 5 degrees. Reproducibility information is substantially redistributed and reduced in important areas.

R1.justification: V2 adds BSC-Nav to the memory-design comparison, describes MemoryVLA as concurrent, and expands benchmark positioning through a platform-comparison table and references including ProcTHOR, HomeRobot, and InfiniteWorld. The GPT-4 reference is removed. The broader VLA and mobile-manipulation positioning remains.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites benchmark construction and real-world interpretation, reverses the related-work subsection order, adds a dataset-distribution subsection, and incorporates RK into the main experimental narrative. The separate appendix structure disappears. The title and author information also change, although most of the model description remains closely matched.

P2.justification: The paper switches from two-column to single-column layout. V2 replaces Figure 1's control-paradigm comparison with memory-design comparisons, redraws the architecture, replaces dataset bars with donut charts, and adds a data-engine diagram and comparison/sensitivity tables. Real-world rollouts incorporate RK and EnP, while numerous appendix displays disappear.

improvement.justification: V2 gains useful memory-parameter sensitivity evidence, cross-room evaluation, and more explicit failure discussion. However, it loses the detailed training recipe and supporting horizon and retrieval analyses. The larger headline margin comes from unexplained revisions to π0.5's scores, and the new noise/occlusion explanations lack dedicated tests. These benefits and losses leave the net quality direction uncertain, particularly the balance between expanded evaluation and reduced reproducibility.
